sections.heading: Dialogue I, Knot iv (printed pp. 32–37)
rows: [p. 32] [Margin: Nodus IV. De loci immobilitate.] Ereu. Neque ego memoriae vitio sed beneficio sententiam illam innominatam praetermisi, cum quam opposui infinito demonstrationem, eandem una opera pessumdederit.

[p. 32] [Margin: Knot IV. On the immobility of place [loci].] Ereu. Nor did I pass over that unnamed opinion [sententiam] by a fault but by a benefit of memory, since the demonstration which I opposed to the infinite has sent the same [opinion] to ruin [pessumdederit] by one [and the same] effort [una opera].

Andab. Ergone putas haec tam impune auferre? vel nescis quanto te commiseris periculo? Quomodo enim loci immobilitatem tuendo satis eris, cum praeter spatium quod imaginarium dicunt, nihil sit, quod immotum consistat? Praeterea quomodo Animam, et si qui sunt abstracti spiritus, locis accommodabis, cum nihil tamen notius sit quam quod Aniculis puerisque certum est, quod nusquam est idem non esse.

Andab. Do you therefore think [that you] carry off these things so unpunished [impune]? or do you not know to how great a danger you have committed yourself? For how will you be sufficient for defending the immobility of place, since besides the space which they call imaginary, there is nothing which stands [consistat] unmoved? Besides, how will you accommodate the Soul [Animam], and, if there are any, abstract spirits, to places, since nevertheless nothing is more known than what is certain to little old women [Aniculis] and boys: that what is nowhere, the same is not.

Ereu. Gravia quidem obiicis, Andabata, sed si patienter mecum agas, omnia tibi reddam expedita. [Margin: Quomodo intellectus res apprehendat.] Hoc itaque cumprimis memento, voces nostras a mente originem trahere eiusque primario referre naturam: Mentem vero plerumque nihil unum absolutumve in sese [p. 33] depictum habere, sed comparando plura, notitias quasi compositas singulorum continere. Unde est ut plurimum aberrent ii, qui ab intellectu ad rerum naturam gradum sibi facientes, eadem quae in intellectu inveniunt, in rebus postea requirant:

Ereu. Weighty things indeed you object, Andabata, but if you deal patiently with me, I will render all things to you disentangled [expedita]. [Margin: How the understanding [intellectus] apprehends things.] This therefore remember first of all [cumprimis]: that our words [voces] draw [their] origin from the mind and primarily refer [referre] its nature; but that the mind for the most part has nothing one or absolute [absolutumve] painted in itself, [p. 33] but by comparing several [things] contains notices [notitias] as it were composite of single [things]. Whence it is that those err very much [plurimum; or 'ut plurimum' = for the most part], who, making for themselves a step from the understanding [intellectu] to the nature of things, afterwards require in things the same things which they find in the understanding:

[Margin: Quomodo immobilitas rei mobili connectatur.] hinc est quod aliqui locum superficiem immobilem audientes, statim in rebus investigant superficiem aliquam quae ex sua natura immobilitatem sit sortita: neque usquam eam reperientes male definitum esse locum clamitent; non attendentes posse huic superficiei ab intellectu notionem immobilitatis contingere ab extrinseco quam ex sese non habet; non sic ut ipsa in re immobilis fiat; sed ut per coniunctionem ad immobile aliquid ipsa in individuo fluens in communi aliqua ratione, consistentiam habeat.

[Margin: How immobility is connected to a mobile thing.] hence it is that some, hearing [that] place [is] an immobile surface [superficiem], at once investigate in things some surface which from its own nature has obtained [sit sortita] immobility: and, finding it nowhere, keep crying out [clamitent] that place has been badly defined; not attending that to this surface the notion of immobility, which it does not have from itself, can befall [contingere] from the understanding, from outside [ab extrinseco]; not so that it itself becomes immobile in the thing [in re = in reality]; but so that through conjunction to something immobile, it, itself flowing in the individual [in individuo], may have consistency [consistentiam] in some common reason [ratione].

Nonne vides Rumum nostrum perpetua successione inconstantem; de quo tamen si dixero aquam propter has aedes quam sub ponte profundiorem habere, vide quomodo nova semper aqua succedente Rumus inconstans constantem propositionem facit. Hoc itaque imprimis statutum sit, fluentem etiam superficiem immobilem esse posse, si ab intellectu, communis aliqua ipsius ratio ad immobile aliquid alligetur.

Do you not see our Rumon [Rumum], inconstant by perpetual succession? of which nevertheless if I shall have said that it has deeper water beside [propter] these houses than under the bridge, see how, new water always succeeding, the inconstant Rumon makes a constant proposition. This therefore first of all [imprimis] let it be established: that even a flowing surface can be immobile, if by the understanding some common reason [ratio] of it is tied to something immobile.

[Margin: Quomodo immobilitas ex re mobili desumatur.] Est et aliud quod postulem, neque puto te gravate concessurum: videlicet non quod est mobile statim omnem in partem esse [p. 34] mobile, sed immobilitatem aliquam cum alia mobilitate tueri posse. Quod recta fertur ab extremo unde proficiscitur, eandem semper occupat partem, quod circulo, centrum aequidistans sibi servat, et in quolibet fere motu aliquam immobilitatem pronum est invenire.

[Margin: How immobility is taken [desumatur] from a mobile thing.] There is also another thing which I would demand [postulem], nor do I think that you will concede [it] grudgingly [gravate]: namely, that what is mobile is not straightway mobile in every part [omnem in partem = in every direction], [p. 34] but can keep [tueri] some immobility with another mobility. What is borne straight [recta] occupies always the same part [partem] from the extreme whence it sets out; what [is borne] in a circle keeps the centre equidistant to itself; and in almost any motion whatever it is easy [pronum] to find some immobility.

Ex quo hunc gradum ad locum facio, ut neque illud undequaque immobile esse necesse sit, quod superficiei, quam locum appellamus, immobilitatem commodat. Et ad rem ipsam nos applicantes, rerum parvarum et facile mobilium loca primo modo designamus. Cum enim de homine, vel veste, vel alia aliqua re transferibili sine labore quaeritur ubi sit, proximum circumstans quod vel in se vel quoad nos immobilitatem habet, nominamus, asserentes in area, in cubiculo, in aedibus, in agro, in urbe, in tali regione esse; superficiem eam proxime contingentem et perpetuo fluentem, re immobili addita in communem trahendo, stabilientes.

From which I make this step to place: that neither is it necessary that that be on every side [undequaque] immobile which lends [commodat] immobility to the surface which we call place. And applying ourselves to the matter itself, we designate the places of small and easily mobile things in the first mode. For when it is asked about a man, or a garment, or some other thing transferable without labour, where it is [ubi sit], we name the nearest surrounding [thing] which, either in itself or as regards us [quoad nos], has immobility, asserting [it] to be in the courtyard [area], in the bedchamber, in the house [aedibus], in the field, in the city, in such a region; establishing [stabilientes] that surface, nearest touching [contingentem] and perpetually flowing, by drawing [it] into a common [reason] [in communem], an immobile thing having been added.

Etsi enim aer qui in aedibus nunc est, expellatur situmque mutet, hoc tamen complexum (aer aedium) stantibus aedibus constans est, neque situm mutare potest. Quod si de re maiori quaestio fiat, posteriori potissimum modo rationem loci designamus. Ut si aedium, vel urbis, vel regionis, vel maris situs investigetur penes stellarum ortus occasusque formamus loci intentionem. Ut cum regio-[p. 35]nem per ea describimus quae ab Ortu, Occasu, Septentrione et Austro ei coniunguntur, per Poli aequatorisve elationem et depressionem et similia. Quoniam enim constans est siderum motus, certisque reversibus certas terrae plagas feriunt, per hos ipsos motus designare certam terrae portionem et potest humana mens et consuevit.

For although the air which is now in the house be expelled and change [its] site [situm], nevertheless this complex [complexum] ('the air of the house'), the house standing, is constant, nor can it change [its] site. But if the question be made about a greater thing, we designate the reason [rationem] of place chiefly in the latter mode. As, if the site of a house, or of a city, or of a region, or of a sea be investigated, we form the intention [intentionem] of place according to [penes] the risings and settings of the stars. As when we describe a region [p. 35] through those things which are joined to it from the East, the West, the North and the South, through the elevation and depression of the Pole or of the equator, and similar things. For since the motion of the stars [siderum] is constant, and with certain returns [reversibus] they strike certain tracts [plagas] of the earth [terrae], through these very motions the human mind both can and has been accustomed to designate a certain portion of the earth [terrae].

Vides itaque loci immobilitatem non in re tantummodo mobili, sed quasi in contemptum materiei et motus, ab ipso motu extrahi et sublimari. Adde his si libet loci immobilitatem non eam esse quam contradictio sit enixa, sed talem quae humano usui actionique serviat et sit idonea.

You see therefore that the immobility of place, not only in a mobile thing, but as it were in contempt of matter [materiei] and motion, is extracted and sublimated [sublimari] from motion itself. Add to these, if it pleases, that the immobility of place is not that which contradiction has brought forth [sit enixa], but such as serves and is fit for human use and action.

[Margin: Spiritus non esse proprie in loco.] Quod incorporeorum locum attinet, nescio an inter Physicos quaeri oporteat vel Theologorum, aut certe Metaphysicorum qui abstractorum scientias excolunt operas ea inquisitio poscat. Unum tamen omittere non possum, Axioma quod ab Aniculis puerisque collegisti, ad eosdem si remittas nihil praeter Philosopho homini decorum te acturum.

[Margin: That spirits are not properly [proprie] in place.] As to what pertains to the place of incorporeal [things], I do not know whether it ought to be asked among the Physicists, or [whether] that inquiry demands the efforts [operas] of the Theologians, or at least of the Metaphysicians, who cultivate the sciences of abstract [things]. One thing nevertheless I cannot omit: [that] the Axiom which you have collected from little old women and boys, if you send [it] back to the same, you will do nothing beyond [praeter] [what is] becoming [decorum] to a Philosopher man.

Quale enim delirium est a vulgo hominibusque sensu mersis quid de substantiis a concretione materiae alienis censendum sit, accipere? Princeps sui saeculi hoc sapientibus per se notum existimavit incorporea in loco non esse. Idem Scholae parentes censuerunt: Aristoteles mundum in loco non esse. Con-[p. 36]tra hos et horum similes trahenda sunt, si Deo placet, a mentibus in coeno sepultis axiomata. Et tamen quam voluminosis gloriantur operibus qui similia nobis axiomata obtrudunt?

For what sort of delirium is it to receive from the vulgar, and from men sunk in sense, what must be judged about substances foreign to the concretion [concretione] of matter? The Prince of his age reckoned this [to be] known through itself to the wise: that incorporeal [things] are not in place. The parents of the School judged the same: Aristotle, that the world is not in place. Against [p. 36] these and [men] similar to these, axioms are to be drawn, if it pleases God, from minds buried in mud [coeno]. And yet in how voluminous works do they glory, who thrust upon us similar axioms?

Uno itaque verbo de substantiis separatis quae dicuntur, derivato per Analogiam nomine et ea quae ex consilio dicitur, aequivocatione dici habeto. Cum enim corpora non sint, superficies superficiebus applicatas in iis expectare fas non est. Quicquid autem aliter de loco dicitur translatione vocis, non proprietate dici certus esto.

In one word therefore, hold that the things which are said about separated substances are said by a name derived through Analogy, and by that equivocation which is called [equivocation] from deliberation [ex consilio]. For since they are not bodies, it is not lawful [fas] to expect in them surfaces applied to surfaces. But whatever is said otherwise about place, be certain that it is said by transference [translatione] of the word [vocis], not by propriety [proprietate].

Asphal. Dum tu Andabatae rationem reddis, nescio quid mihi in mentem venit de celebri quadam quaestione, quae aetherem quemdam purissimum per omnia corpora diffundi disputat; num, inquam, non hac ipsa demonstratione, sicut de vacuo, sic etiam de ipsa sententia lata sit, vel certe mediocri opera ferri possit.

Asphal. While you render an account [rationem] to Andabata, something [nescio quid] comes into my mind about a certain celebrated question, which disputes [whether] a certain most pure aether is diffused through all bodies: whether, I say, by this very demonstration, just as about the vacuum, so also about it sentence [sententia] has not been passed [lata sit], or at least can be passed [ferri] with moderate effort.

Ereu. Ea difficultas duos labores continet; alter est, an fluidum quidpiam toto sit orbe diffusum quicquid illud sit, homogeneum an pluribus distinctum naturis? Reliquus id petit an tale liquidum unius subtilitatis sit et ingenii, aetherque appellandus? an vero iuxta solidorum ad quae appellitur, naturam, ipsum etiam varias indoles trahat. Et ad hanc posteriorem inquisitionem, {?alia} congerenda sunt [p. 37] principia.

Ereu. That difficulty contains two labours: the one is, whether some fluid is diffused through the whole orb [orbe], whatever it be, homogeneous or distinguished by several natures? The remaining [one] asks this: whether such a liquid is of one subtlety and character [ingenii], and is to be called aether? or whether, according to the nature of the solids to which it is driven [appellitur], it itself also draws various dispositions [indoles]. And for this latter inquiry other {?alia} [p. 37] principles must be gathered together.

Sed priorem (saltem ex parte) dirimit dicta demonstratio: [Margin: Naturam liquidam aliquam esse.] clarum enim est corpora minima (quod in omni generatione usu venire necesse est) moveri, et in unum corpus convenire non posse absque liquidi alicuius medii vehiculo. Unde atomi Epicurei etiam ex hac parte deficiunt. Cum enim divisibiles sint, manifestum est quoties conveniunt, vacuum aut liquidum mixtum habere, cum eorum figurae non semper locum repleant: quod si facerent, neque satis variabiles figuras haberent ad compositorum varietatem, quae ex iis expectatur, fingendam, et ipsi uno quasi corpore moverentur; neque generationi possent accommodari. Sed uno verbo proferam quod sentio, nusquam ego motum neque lationem sine fluido aliquo medio effectum crediderim.

But the former [one] (at least in part) the said demonstration settles [dirimit]: [Margin: That there is some liquid nature.] for it is clear that the smallest bodies (which it is necessary should come into use [usu venire] in every generation) cannot be moved and come together into one body without the vehicle of some liquid medium. Whence the Epicurean atoms also fail on this side. For since they are divisible [divisibiles], it is manifest that as often as they come together they have a vacuum or liquid mixed [in], since their figures do not always fill up the place: and if they did so, neither would they have figures variable enough for fashioning [fingendam] the variety of composites which is expected from them, and they themselves would be moved as it were as one body; nor could they be accommodated to generation. But in one word I will utter what I feel [sentio]: nowhere would I believe motion or carriage [lationem] to be effected without some fluid medium.

Andab. Hac in parte ignosce, si quod verum est libere dicam aperte te errare. Quid enim receptius in omni Philosophia quam ingentes illos coelorum orbes unum infra alium absque ullo intermedio liquido perpetua et infatigabili volutatione circumferri: liquidum enim aetherem inter immortales substantias collocare quantum absurdi est?

Andab. In this part pardon [me], if I say freely what is true, [that] you openly err. For what is more received in all Philosophy than that those huge orbs of the heavens, one below another, without any intermediate liquid, are carried round with perpetual and unwearying rolling [volutatione]: for to place a liquid aether among immortal substances, how much of absurdity is it?

terms: Literally 'give to the bottom' (pessum dare); one demonstration (against the infinite, Knot ii) is said also to have destroyed the unnamed opinion of Philoponus' subsistent dimensions mentioned at the end of Knot iii.

Aristotle, Physics IV.4 (212a20): place is 'the first immobile limit of the surrounding body'. The scholastic difficulty is that the surrounding surface (of air, of water) is always changing; White's solution is that immobility is conferred on the flowing surface by the understanding, by relating it to something immobile.
The 'surface of the surrounding body' in the Aristotelian definition of place.
the space which they call imaginary
Late-scholastic extramundane 'imaginary space' (see glossary, Knot iii); Andabata's point is that only it, being nothing, would be truly unmoved.
Proverbial for unlearned common opinion; the 'axiom' that what is nowhere is not (cf. Augustine's and the schoolmen's discussion of 'nusquam'). Ereunius turns the phrase back on Andabata on p. 35.
Logical vox: a significant word, which (Aristotle, De interpretatione 1) signifies the concepts of the mind and only through them things; hence 'our words draw their origin from the mind'.
White's (and Digby's) theory that most concepts are relational, formed by comparing several things; the 'immobility' of place is such a comparative notion.
Scholastic denominatio extrinseca: a thing is named from something not in it (as a wall is 'seen'). The surface is 'immobile' by extrinsic denomination.
in the individual / in a common reason
The surface as this individual flows; under a common notion ('the water by this house', 'the air of the house') it is constant.
Could be read as a common noun, but it is personified as a river with water deeper by 'these houses' than under 'the bridge'.

Rumon was the archaic name of the Tiber (Servius on Aeneid 8.63, 8.90; Festus): 'our Rumon' places the conversation in Rome, by the river. White was in Rome in the 1630s–40s. The example is a version of Heraclitus' river.
A proposition about the river remains true though its subject's matter flows: the logical model for the immobility of place.
pars here = 'direction', 'side' (in partem = towards a side).
The point is directional: a straight mover keeps the same direction (eandem partem), a circular one keeps the same distance to the centre.
in the first mode / in the latter mode
Two ways of designating place: by the nearest immobile surrounding (room, house, city) and by reference to the stars (latitude, longitude, cardinal points).
Scholastic: what is immobile not absolutely but for human purposes; cf. the end of the paragraph, 'immobility … fit for human use and action'.
Logical complexum: a term made of several words ('aer aedium'), as opposed to an incomplexum; it signifies a constant item though its matter changes.
Also the Aristotelian category 'position' (situs/positio); here simply location.
Scholastic intentio = concept formed by the mind (cf. glossary 'intention').
the elevation and depression of the Pole or of the equator
Geographical latitude: the altitude of the celestial pole (equivalently of the equator) above the horizon.
Of the regular return of stars to rising and setting.
Classical for a zone of the earth or heaven.
Also the alchemical term for refining by vaporizing; place's immobility is 'extracted and sublimated' out of motion, a chemical metaphor.
enitor = 'strive, struggle' or 'bring forth (a child)'; also possible 'which contradiction has struggled for'.
I.e. not an absolute immobility whose opposite would be a contradiction, but a practical one. The construction is unusual; the sense is clear.
Proper vs transferred (metaphorical, translatio) use of a word: spirits are 'in place' only improperly.
praeter = 'beyond', 'contrary to', 'except'; so 'nothing contrary to what becomes a philosopher'.
Ironical litotes: sending the axiom back to old women and boys is the only thing fitting for a philosopher. Cicero's decorum (De officiis I.27).
Ciceronian (Tusculans I.66, 'nihil concretum') for bodily composition; separated substances are 'foreign' to it.
Boethius, De hebdomadibus: among the 'common conceptions of the mind' known only to the learned (docti) is 'incorporalia in loco non esse'. White's 'sapientibus per se notum' echoes this exactly.
Here Aristotle: the world (the outermost heaven) is not in place, Physics IV.5 (212b8–22).
aequivocatio a consilio = 'deliberate equivocation', as opposed to a casu ('by chance').
Boethius (In Categorias) divides equivocals into a casu and a consilio; analogical names (like 'healthy') are of the deliberate kind. White: 'place' of spirits is said analogically, not univocally.
Classical rhetorical term for metaphor (translatio = μεταφορά).
the things which are said … are said
The relative 'quae dicuntur' could also attach to 'substantiis separatis' ('substances which are called separated'), but then 'dici' has no subject.
White's point: all predicates (including 'in place') said of spirits are analogical, not univocal.
Legal idiom; Asphalius asks whether the demonstration against the vacuum also 'gives verdict' on the question of a universal aether.
aether purissimus per omnia corpora diffusus
a most pure aether diffused through all bodies
The current 'celebrated question' of a subtle fluid pervading all bodies and the heavens (Stoic pneuma; Kepler, Descartes' subtle matter, Digby's and Gassendi's debates).
'toto orbe' could mean 'the whole world (universe)' or the celestial orbs; kept 'orb' (glossary).
ingenium usually 'wit' (glossary) but here of a thing = 'natural quality'; indoles = 'innate nature'.
Departure from the glossary rendering 'wit', since a liquid is meant.
from appello, -ere (3rd conj.) = 'drive to', 'bring to land'; not appello, -are 'call'.
The aether takes on dispositions from the solids it washes against.
Aristotelian-scholastic minima and the corpuscles of Digby's natural philosophy; generation requires their meeting in a liquid vehicle.
Revived by Gassendi in the 1640s; White argues they need a vacuum or an interstitial fluid.
Aristotle's term for locomotion, Physics VII–VIII.
The heavens as incorruptible (Aristotle, De caelo I.3): Andabata's Peripatetic objection, which Knot v answers.
notes: Unit: Dialogue I, Knot iv, complete in one part. PDF pp. 43–48 = printed pp. 32–37. It begins on p. 32 at Ereunius' 'Neque ego memoriae vitio sed beneficio' (margin 'Nodus IV. De loci immobilitate'), as FM2's table says (p. 32). It ends with Andabata's question '…quantum absurdi est?' on p. 37. Below it, Ereunius' 'Ast ego tibi hoc polliceor' begins Knot v (margin 'Nodus V. Substantiam aliquam …'). FM2's table gives p. 38 for Knot v, but the margin puts its start at the foot of p. 37 (PDF 48): following the book, the next unit starts there. The offset of +11 holds (p. 37 = PDF 48).

Rows: one row per speech; Ereunius' long speech on pp. 32–36 is split at sentence breaks and at the marginal headings so Latin and English line up. Printed page breaks are marked [p. n]. Marginal notes: 'Nodus IV. De loci immobilitate' (p. 32), 'Quomodo intellectus res apprehendat' (p. 32), 'Quomodo immobilitas rei mobili cōnectatur' (p. 33), 'Quomodo immobilitas ex re mobili desumatur' (p. 33), 'Spiritus non esse proprie in loco' (p. 35), 'Naturam liquidam aliquam esse' (p. 37, printed 'Naturā liquidā aliquā esse').

Conventions as in glossary.md: long s → s; æ/œ → ae/oe; tildes expanded (cōmiseris → commiseris, cōnectatur → connectatur); 'vl.' (p. 33) expanded as videlicet; consonantal u → v; accents dropped; '&' → et. Spellings kept as printed: 'obiicis', 'cumprimis', 'materiei', 'expectare', 'coeno', 'Epicurei', 'quidpiam'.

Printed/sense notes: (a) p. 34, 'quodvel' is printed as one word; read 'quod vel'. (b) p. 36, 'Andabatę' (e-caudata) is read as dative 'Andabatae' ('render an account to Andabata'): Ereunius, not Andabata, was speaking, so a vocative 'Andabata' would not fit. (c) p. 37, 'Cum enim divisibiles sint' of the Epicurean atoms: atoms are by definition indivisible, and the argument (their rigid figures cannot fill all place) suits 'indivisibiles'; possibly a misprint, but kept as printed and translated 'divisible'. (d) p. 32, Andabata's speech ends with a full stop though it continues his questions; kept. (e) 'Rumus' (p. 33) is taken as Rumon, the old name of the Tiber (see terms). (f) p. 34, 'in communem trahendo' is elliptical; '[reason]' (rationem) supplied from p. 33 'in communi aliqua ratione'.

Uncertain: p. 36, 'alia congerenda sunt principia': the second letter is broken in the scan and could be 'alta' ('deep principles must be gathered'); read {?alia}. Margin p. 33 'ex re inobili' shows a damaged m; read 'mobili' (the sense, 'from a mobile thing', requires it). No illegible words.

Verification pass: the transcription was compared again with the page images (300 dpi crops of pp. 33, 34, 36, 37), and the English with the Latin, sentence by sentence (cases, tenses, moods, negatives, comparatives, omissions). This gave 6 corrections: (1) p. 33, 'Unde est ut plurimum aberrent ii': the bracket now gives the alternative reading of 'ut plurimum' as the set phrase 'for the most part'. (2) p. 36, 'Uno itaque verbo de substantiis separatis quae dicuntur … dici habeto' had been rendered with '[place]' supplied as subject and 'quae dicuntur' as 'which are called separated'; corrected to 'the things which are said about separated substances are said …', with no supplied subject. (3) p. 36, 'pluribus distinctum naturis' (ablative) had been rendered 'distinguished into several natures'; corrected to 'by several natures'. (4) p. 37, 'Sed uno verbo proferam quod sentio' had been rendered as a purpose clause ('that I may utter'); corrected to the main-clause 'I will utter'. (5) p. 36, an exclamation mark added in the English after 'buried in mud' was removed to follow the printed full stop. (6) p. 36–37, the page marker [p. 37] was moved to fall before 'principles', where the Latin page turns; also 'in re' given its alternative sense 'in reality'. Transcription: no changes; 'alia' (p. 36) remains uncertain.
